title: Brown Planthopper: Symptoms, Hopperburn and Control
metaTitle: Brown Planthopper: Hopperburn Symptoms and Control
metaDescription: The brown planthopper can dry out whole patches of palay. See its symptoms, why careless spraying causes outbreaks, and how to control it safely.
excerpt: The brown planthopper, Nilaparvata lugens, is a tiny brown insect that sucks sap at the base of the rice plant. In Tagalog it is kayumangging ngusong kabayo. When its numbers explode, whole patches of palay dry up in a condition called hopperburn. In 2017 it damaged rice in 18 provinces.

heroImage.alt: A long winged brown planthopper, Nilaparvata lugens, resting on a green leaf
heroImage.credit: portioid, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

blocks.text: What the brown planthopper is

Planthoppers are small insects that suck plant sap. Two kinds attack rice: the brown planthopper, or BPH, and the whitebacked planthopper, Sogatella furcifera. You will also see the name written as brown plant hopper, in two words. Its Tagalog names are kayumangging ngusong kabayo and kayumangging hanip, and it is also called hanip sa palay. Farmers use hanip for other tiny pests as well, which our page on [hanip, mites and aphids](/pests/hanip-mites-and-aphids) covers.

The adult is only 2.5 to 3 millimeters long. Some adults have long wings and fly to lights, while others have short wings and stay on the plant. Females lay eggs in batches inside the leaf sheath and the midrib. The brown nymphs molt five times before they become adults.
Brown plant hopper symptoms

BPH feeds at the base of the tillers, so look low. Often, the first sign is yellowing plants. As numbers climb, the leaves turn orange yellow, then brown and dry. Heavy infestation leaves round patches of dead, dried plants. That is hopperburn, and at that level the crop loss can reach 100 percent. The usual loss is 10 to 50 percent or more per hectare.

items: Honeydew and black sooty mold on the lower stems
Hoppers crowded on the base of the tillers, dropping onto the water when you tap the hill
Crescent shaped white eggs inside the midrib or leaf sheath, with egg laying marks that let fungi and bacteria in
Short, stunted hills sick with ragged stunt or grassy stunt, two viruses BPH carries that no spray can cure

blocks.text: Hopperburn looks a lot like the bugburn caused by the [rice black bug](/pests/rice-black-bug). The check is the sooty mold at the base of the plant, which planthopper attacks leave.
Why brown planthopper outbreaks happen

Put plainly, planthoppers are not pests until you apply insecticides carelessly. In a healthy field, spiders, mirid bugs, water striders, small wasps and other natural enemies keep BPH in check. Early or needless sprays kill these predators. Then the hopper eggs hatch unchecked and the population explodes. This is a main cause of outbreaks, along with long winged hoppers that the wind carries in.

A 1986 study in South Cotabato, reported by Agriculture Monthly, showed it in the field. After insecticide sprays against leaf eating caterpillars, the spiders dropped and BPH numbers climbed sharply.
Other things that favor BPH

items: Too much nitrogen, such as extra [urea fertilizer](/blog/urea-fertilizer), which softens the plant
Dense planting and a closed, humid canopy
Direct seeded fields, which suffer more than transplanted ones

blocks.text: BPH counts climb highest near harvest. In the wet season that is most often September to October, and in the dry season March to April. The 2017 outbreak across 18 provinces caused an estimated 17.87 million pesos in damage.
How to monitor the planthopper

items.title: Check the seedbed daily
items.text: Make daily checks in the seedbed and weekly checks in the field. Look along each side of the seedbed.

items.title: Tap the base
items.text: Grasp a hill, bend it over slightly and tap it near the base. Count the hoppers that fall onto the water.

items.title: Walk diagonally
items.text: In transplanted rice, cross the field corner to corner and look at the base of 10 to 20 hills along the way.

items.title: Count the helpers too
items.text: Note the spiders and other predators. If natural enemies outnumber the hoppers, the risk of hopperburn is low.

items.title: Stop at the milk stage
items.text: Once the grain reaches the milk stage, you can stop checking for BPH.

blocks.text:
At one BPH per stem or less, you still have time to act if numbers rise. Drain the field for three to four days once counts reach about 10 per hill, since BPH prefers cool, humid conditions at the base.

A light trap can warn you early: set it against a pale wall or above a basin of water. If hundreds of BPH land in it, check your seedbed and fields at once and scout daily for the next few weeks. Keep the lights away from seedbeds and fields.

anee.io helps you keep that rhythm. Your [cropping calendar](/features/cropping-calendar) counts days after transplanting for every lot, so you can set a weekly hopper check from early tillering to the milk stage. The [growth stages](/features/growth-stages-and-weather) view shows when each lot enters its risky weeks. Snap a photo of the insects at the base and send it to Anee, the [smart farm technician](/features/ai-agricultural-technician), who helps you tell a planthopper from a leafhopper in Tagalog or English.
Management that keeps BPH down
Resistant varieties

These are BPH resistant varieties: PSB Rc2, PSB Rc10, and NSIC Rc212, Rc222, Rc224, Rc226, Rc298, Rc300 and Rc308. Ask your Municipal Agriculture Office which ones suit your area, and see our guide to [rice varieties in the Philippines](/crops/rice-varieties-philippines).

Resistance does not last forever. IR26, the first BPH resistant variety, lost its resistance in 1976 to 1977 when a new BPH biotype appeared. IR36, with a different resistance gene, held for 14 years. So combine resistant seed with the practices below.
Cultural control

items: Where BPH is attacking, plant a resistant variety and transplant. Do not broadcast the seed during an attack.
Plant together with your neighbors and leave a one to two month fallow between crops to break the BPH life cycle.
Use 20 by 20 centimeter spacing, because dense planting raises planthopper numbers.
Split nitrogen into three applications, as in our guide to [fertilizer for rice](/blog/fertilizer-for-rice).

Irrigate by alternate wetting and drying, or AWD. It works with split nitrogen against BPH. Start it 21 to 30 days after transplanting, and add water only when the observation well, a perforated bamboo or PVC tube set in the paddy, has run dry.
Keep potassium adequate. More [potash](/blog/potash-fertilizer) makes the plant less susceptible.
Raise the water from time to time to drown eggs at the base, and alternate drying and flooding at the milk stage.
Flood the seedbed for a day so only the seedling tips show. This controls BPH there.
Plow under ratoons and volunteer rice after harvest.

blocks.text: Do not spray early

Do not spray in the first 30 days after transplanting or 40 days after seeding. The plants recover from early damage by making new leaves and tillers. Early sprays also stop friendly insects from settling in the field.
When to spray for brown planthopper

blocks.caption: Brown planthopper counts and what to do
rows: No insecticide. Keep scouting every week
A recommended insecticide may be used, by its label

blocks.text: Between those two counts, keep scouting each week and let the predators work. Our guide on [when to spray rice pests](/blog/when-to-spray-rice-pests) puts these numbers next to the other rice pests, so you can plan the whole season.

blocks.title: Hopperburn does not always mean spray
blocks.text: Do not spray even rice already hit by hopperburn if natural enemies outnumber the planthoppers. Count both before you mix anything.
Chemical control with pymetrozine

Use insecticide only as a last resort, and choose a selective one if the infestation is very high. In a seedbed, spray only if all three are true: the stems average over one planthopper each, hoppers outnumber their natural enemies, and you cannot flood the seedbed.

Pymetrozine is a common choice. It belongs to IRAC Group 9B, and it stops the hoppers from feeding. Chess insecticide (Chess 50 WG) from Syngenta contains pymetrozine, and its Philippine product page lists brown plant hopper on rice. Syngenta calls it highly selective for beneficial insects. Insect growth regulators also work against the nymphs.

Treat these as examples. Follow the label and the FPA registration, and never add a broad spectrum insecticide to the tank just to be sure. Our guide to [Alika, Virtako and Chess](/blog/rice-insecticides-alika-virtako-chess) compares these products.

blocks.text: Brown planthopper questions

items.q: What does a brown planthopper look like?
items.a: A small brown insect, 2.5 to 3 millimeters long, sitting at the base of the tillers. Tap the hill and many drop onto the water.

items.q: What are the first brown plant hopper symptoms?
items.a: Yellowing plants, then leaves turning orange yellow and brown, with honeydew and sooty mold on the lower stems. Round patches of dried plants mean hopperburn.

items.q: Why did BPH attack after I sprayed?
items.a: Broad spectrum sprays kill the spiders and other predators that eat planthoppers, so the hopper eggs hatch with nothing to stop them. This is a main trigger of outbreaks.

items.q: Which insecticide is for the brown planthopper?
items.a: Pymetrozine, as in Chess 50 WG, is one example with brown plant hopper on its Philippine label. Spray only after counting, and follow the label and FPA registration.

items.q: Is the planthopper the same as the green leafhopper?
items.a: No. Leafhoppers usually feed on the leaves, higher up, while planthoppers feed near the base of the tillers. Tap the hill to see which one you have.
